definition: The Catholic Church views artificial intelligence as a significant technological development that must be governed by strict ethical principles rooted in human dignity and the common good.
details: In January 2025, the Church issued the doctrinal note Antiqua et nova co-issued by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and the Dicastery for Culture and Education. It addresses the "relationship between artificial intelligence and human intelligence" and offers reflections on the "anthropological and ethical challenges raised by AI". In August 2025, Time magazine included Pope Leo XIV in its 2025 list of the World’s Most Influential People in Artificial Intelligence. In May 2026, Pope Leo XIV approved the creation of a new Vatican commission on artificial intelligence. He released his first papal encyclical, titled Magnifica humanitas, on the topic later in the month.

explainer.lead: The Catholic Church treats artificial intelligence as a powerful technology whose development should be judged by its effects on human dignity and the common good. Its guidance examines both the relationship between artificial and human intelligence and the ethical questions AI raises, making it relevant to anyone building or deploying consequential systems.

tiers.eli5: Imagine inventing a very clever robot helper: being clever is not enough, because it also needs to treat people well and help the whole community. The Catholic Church applies that idea to AI. It asks people to think carefully about what makes humans special and whether new technology respects them.
tiers.practitioner: For an engineer, this is a normative ethical lens rather than an implementation method or software standard. Antiqua et nova, issued in January 2025 by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and the Dicastery for Culture and Education, can inform reviews of human oversight, social effects, and respect for human dignity. Its broad principles still have to be translated into concrete requirements, tests, and deployment decisions.
tiers.paperLevel: The framework is a normative account of AI grounded in human dignity and the common good, with no mathematical definition or algorithmic procedure. Antiqua et nova examines the relationship between artificial intelligence and human intelligence and addresses the anthropological and ethical challenges raised by AI. Its scope is moral and anthropological evaluation rather than model design or empirical performance measurement.

explainer.example: Before deploying an AI system that makes important decisions about people, a reviewer following this approach would ask whether the system respects each person's dignity and serves the wider community, not merely whether it works efficiently. The review would also consider what the system's use implies about human intelligence and responsibility.

explainer.intuition: Technical capability alone cannot settle whether an AI system is good for people. The Church evaluates it through moral purposes and human consequences, especially dignity and the common good.
howItWorks: Recognize AI as a significant technological development rather than treating it as morally neutral or automatically beneficial.
Examine how artificial intelligence relates to human intelligence.
Identify the anthropological and ethical challenges created by a particular use of AI.
Assess those challenges against human dignity and the common good.
Express the resulting guidance through doctrinal notes, papal teaching, and Vatican institutions.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives AI debates a moral vocabulary centered on people and society rather than capability alone. Engagement has continued through Antiqua et nova, Pope Leo XIV's inclusion in Time's August 2025 AI influence list, his approval of a Vatican AI commission in May 2026, and his encyclical Magnifica humanitas later that month.
misconceptions: It is not simply a rejection of AI; the Church treats it as a significant development requiring ethical governance.
It is not a technical specification for building or benchmarking AI systems.
The Church's engagement is not limited to one document; it also includes later papal teaching and a Vatican commission.
